question: A platform team wants a /release-notes slash command that every engineer on the repository gets automatically after git pull, so nobody has to reinstall it manually. Where should the team save the command file?
options: A) Save it to ~/.claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md so that Claude loads the command automatically in every project the team lead opens on their machine.
B) Save it to .claude/commands/release-notes.md inside the project and commit that file to the shared repository so it distributes through version control.
C) Save it to ~/.claude/commands/release-notes.md on the team lead's machine and have each engineer copy the file to their own local ~/.claude/commands/ directory.
D) Save it to .claude/commands/release-notes.md in the project root, but add that file to .gitignore so each engineer's local changes stay conflict-free.
correct_answers: B) Save it to .claude/commands/release-notes.md inside the project and commit that file to the shared repository so it distributes through version control.
explanations: Incorrect. The ~/.claude/skills/ directory is personal to the team lead's machine and is not tracked by version control. This approach only loads the command in the lead's own projects and does not share it with the team.

Correct. Project-scoped commands stored in .claude/commands/ inside the project root are normal repository files. Committing the file ensures that every engineer receives it automatically via git pull with no additional manual steps.

Incorrect. Saving the slash command file in the user-scoped ~/.claude/commands/ directory means it only works on the team lead's machine. Even if other engineers manually copy it, the process defeats the goal of automatic, git-based distribution after a pull.
Incorrect. Adding the file to .gitignore prevents it from ever being committed to the shared repository. As a result, pulling the repository will not deliver the command to any other engineer.
